title: In/tension modeling: what gives us the right?
text:
In/tension modeling: what gives us the right?

In/Tension modeling: What gives us the right?

How to navigate opposing voices and lived tensions.

By Julia Beard, Naman Mandhan, & Stacie Sheldon

Asking the Hardest Question First

“What gives us the right to make the interventions and choices we are contemplating on behalf of others?” asks Erika Hall, cofounder of Mule Design. For UX professionals, it’s a question worth sitting with. We’re driven by empathy and a desire to solve problems, yet it’s not common practice for us to question our own authority. How often do we stop to ask the question Erika poses — especially when so much of our job involves putting solutions out into the world? In our effort to do good, we risk unintentionally causing harm. Do we recognize how much power and privilege come with that responsibility?

In Part One of In/Tension Modeling as a UX research and strategy tool, we explored the reality that when you solve one problem, other problems are naturally created. We also discussed how, while analyzing data, you will often find perspectives that are in conflict with one another, and how it is vital to amplify all perspectives, not just the loud ones.

In this Part Two, we go a step deeper into how In/Tension Modeling can be applied to anticipate, prevent, and respond to potential harms while creating solutions. Throughout the design process, it offers a way to continually check the work against Erika’s question: “What gives us the right?” — ensuring that the drive to solve problems is balanced with care for those most affected by the outcomes.

Throughout this article, we share examples of how In/Tension Modeling helped us navigate conflicting perspectives and advocate for the lived experiences of those most affected by the outcomes of a solution. While reading these examples you’ll find moments where we often questioned our own authority on highly polarizing topics. Instead of taking sides, we sought to make space for all the voices and used practical tools to find paths forward that minimize harm. These stories demonstrate that staying with the tension, rather than rushing to resolve it, can lead to more inclusive and resilient outcomes.

How In/Tension Modeling Works: A Quick Map

The stories in this article move through three recurring steps. You’ll see each of them in action as you read.

Step 1: Surface moments of tension

While interacting with research findings, we may encounter opinions or experiences that contradict one another. A common question that arises is how to navigate these conflicting needs and goals, which can feel paralyzing. One effective approach is to juxtapose these perspectives. Doing so allows us to see the full spectrum of needs and goals, leading to better understanding and more informed decision-making. Learn more about this step in Part One of In/Tension Modeling as a UX Research and Strategy Tool.

Step 2: Identify opportunities and cultivate solutions

Where there is tension, there is opportunity. Moments of conflict often reveal pain points, but by reframing those pain points as opportunities, we shift from what is not working to what could work better. This mindset helps us approach problem solving with curiosity instead of frustration, and it keeps conversations constructive.

Once opportunities have been identified, brainstorm ways to address them. Each opportunity becomes a prompt for generating solution ideas that balance the needs and values represented in the voices from research.

Step 3: Assess solution feasibility

Once solutions have been brainstormed, take time to consider how each one might affect all parties involved. A helpful way to do this is by exploring the relationships between conflicting points of view and using the Range of Tolerance tool to see where each voice falls. This helps identify whether a proposed solution might unintentionally exclude or disadvantage someone.

Involving a diverse group at this stage can surface different perspectives and reduce bias. It is also important to remember that solving one problem can sometimes create another. Revisit the preferences and tolerance ranges of each voice to ensure the solution remains balanced and practical.

Repeat step three for all solutions.

Central to Step 3 is a tool designed to make that assessment visible across every voice in the room: the Range of Tolerance.

The Range of Tolerance

The strength of the Range of Tolerance lies in its honesty. Full agreement is rare. Rather than seeking solutions everyone loves, it helps identify solutions that people can genuinely accept while intentionally mitigating harm or exclusion. When a voice falls outside the range of tolerance, it signals that a proposed solution may lead to disengagement, resistance, or loss of participation.

When testing the viability of solutions, the project team looked for options where all voices fall within either the preference zone or the range of tolerance.

  • Preference zone: The proposed solution is ideal for that group.
  • Range of tolerance zone: While the proposed solution may not be their preferred option, they can live with it and it is unlikely to cause harm.
  • Outside both zones: Anything outside the range of tolerance means they are not willing to consent to that solution.

It is difficult to find solutions that place every voice in the preference zone, especially when perspectives are in conflict. But aiming for solutions that keep all voices within the range of tolerance is a practical and powerful goal. It allows us to design with all perspectives in mind, rather than feeling forced to choose one over another; or worse, abandoning the effort to design a solution at all.

Responsible design does not pick sides and does not ignore harms. It works through the tension.

When Every Voice Tells a Different Story: A Case from the Field

Tension isn’t always a bad thing; it can actually bring important truths to the surface. The role of a researcher is not to be a peacekeeper–it is to sit with conflicting insights and find a way forward through them. One project brought this challenge into sharp focus: we were asked to work on one of the most polarizing government programs out there, child support. By design, the program can feel like it creates a winner and a loser. If you are paying support, you may feel you are paying too much or that the money is not being spent as intended. If you are receiving support, you may feel you are not getting nearly enough to meet your family’s needs. Those opposing experiences, both valid, make the program emotionally charged for everyone involved.

Even people who have never participated in the Child Support Program often carry assumptions shaped by what they have heard from friends, family, or the media. Phrases such as “deadbeat parent” or “they get so much in child support, they probably don’t even spend it on the kids” seep into everyday conversations and influence how we see the system, often in ways that are oversimplified or unfair.

Choosing not to act would still leave children bearing the consequences.

For this qualitative research project, our goal was to help child support employees build empathy with families by sharing the stories of people who had lived experience with the program. We also recognized that while navigating child support could be incredibly difficult for participants, the work could be emotionally complex and demanding for staff. Heavy workloads and highly sensitive situations could influence how families experienced the system. We were asked to create a storytelling exhibit to help reconnect staff with the human side of their work. To tell these stories authentically, we first needed to listen.

The foundation of this research was one-on-one interviews with families connected to the program. We spoke with people who pay child support, who receive it, and who do both. We sought a diversity of voices which included moms, dads, family members with guardianship, individuals who had left the program, and participants whose involvement ranged from just one year to over thirty.

As we conducted interviews, we repeatedly heard perspectives that were in direct tension with one another. In one conversation, a parent who pays child support shared that their monthly payments were so high they were being pushed into debt and struggling to maintain a stable home. In the very next interview, a parent who receives child support described that same payment structure as leaving them without enough money to cover basic needs like food, rent, and childcare. Each parent’s experience was real and valid, shaped by their own circumstances, and each revealed how the system could place families in competing positions. Somewhere in the middle of that tension was a child, depending on both.

As a researcher when someone shares a deeply personal experience, especially one that impacts their entire family, you feel a responsibility to honor that. It is not just about listening; it is about carrying their voice forward in a meaningful way. In this case, that responsibility felt heavy. Every possible solution carried a risk. Solving for one group could unintentionally hurt another. And that harm was real. It could mean one group going into overwhelming debt or the other group not having the support needed to care for their family. Choosing not to act would still leave children bearing the consequences.

This led us to consider a framework authored by Designit entitled Do No Harm. The framework challenges practitioners to think about the consequences not only of their actions, but also of their inaction. It encourages us to keep moving forward, even if we make mistakes, as long as we do not become passive.

“If the design discipline is to evolve into a safer and more conscientious version of itself, we need to develop approaches from within to be able to effectively forecast, prevent, and respond to harm. A disciplinary culture shift is in order, and the Do No Harm framework provides a way towards achieving it.” — Dr. Pardis Shafafi​, Global Responsible Business Lead of Designit

After careful reflection, we recognized that doing nothing (not directly addressing the tensions) carried greater consequences than taking action . We chose to adopt the Do No Harm framework with In/Tension Modeling and committed to amplifying the lived experiences we uncovered. That choice gave us a clear path forward; not the easy path, not the fast path, but the honest, difficult, and necessary one. Through In/Tension Modeling, we didn’t just identify points of tension; we stayed with them, worked through them, and sought to fully understand every perspective.

The result was a storytelling exhibit built for program staff, organized around the voices of payers, receivers, and people who had experienced both. It wasn’t designed to declare a winner. It was designed to make the full range of lived experiences impossible to ignore, inviting staff to sit with the people behind the cases rather than the cases alone. The exhibit included reflection questions, guiding principles for engagement, and a call to action for teams ready to do something with what they heard. We built it to last beyond the project. The voices we had been trusted to carry forward were at its heart.

That process, staying with the tension long enough to honor every voice, is what In/Tension Modeling made possible. And it wasn’t the last time we’d need it.

When Empathy Is Not Enough

Even with a strong foundation in empathy and a commitment to honoring every voice, there are moments when progress stalls. Tensions can become so entrenched — politically, emotionally, or institutionally, that traditional methods of facilitation and consensus-building fall short.

In another project with a statewide Child Support Program, we encountered exactly this kind of deeply entrenched disagreement over whether families receiving state assistance should be required to participate in the Program. Despite clear direction and shared intentions, the people involved struggled to move forward. The deeper we went, the more it became evident that no amount of storytelling or surface-level agreement could bridge the divide. We applied In/Tension Modeling not only as a research tool, but as a strategic intervention to help people see one another’s perspectives more clearly, and to begin moving past their entrenched positions.

The disagreement surfaced when we were helping to shape a future vision for how services would be delivered. In the first phase, we conducted research to understand how staff across the program perceived the current system, while also gathering experiences from the families being served. This work revealed a deeply divided landscape. Two dominant narratives had taken hold, and neither side seemed willing or able to move toward common ground.

On one side, some of these stakeholders expressed a desire to change the experience for families receiving state assistance. They described how participation in the program is mandatory for those on assistance, since the state seeks reimbursement through child support collections. Many believe that families often do not understand this requirement when they apply for assistance, or that they lack a real choice because the financial support is essential. Some participants questioned whether this approach truly benefits families, arguing that it can cause harm by reducing autonomy and dignity without generating significant financial return for the state.

At the same time, other stakeholders expressed a different perspective: the program should not change because individuals who use and benefit from the services of the state have an obligation to help repay those costs. For this perspective, required participation was not viewed as punitive but as necessary for fairness, accountability, and in some cases protection. They noted that mandatory engagement with state systems can, in certain situations such as cases of family violence, create opportunities for safety, support, or intervention that might not otherwise occur.

We wondered how to get past this argument. The more it was discussed the more entrenched it felt. We decided a starting point should be to model the two sides of the debate:

As a third party this was our best effort to represent the two sides and we were as intentional as possible to write each voice without bias, knowing that we could not write each side exactly how a person might want to see it represented.

One learning we took from this experience was that, next time, we might invite working groups to participate in creating the models themselves. In our case, we did not have enough time to do so (and it remains to be seen if it would have been beneficial or created a sticking point) but the models as written did produce an immediate response. One person said, “I don’t see my idea on here. There is a loophole where we can avoid forcing them into this program if we wish.” We had never heard that idea before and it became a voice in the middle as well as the beginning of a possible solution for today while the deeper issue is still debated.

Facing Our Own Biases in the Process

While modeling opposing voices in the child support project helped move the conversation forward, it also revealed something we hadn’t anticipated, our own blind spots. As researchers and facilitators, we’re trained to center empathy and maintain neutrality, but the charged nature of this work pushed us into uncomfortable territory.

When tensions mirrored our own deeply held beliefs, it became painfully clear how hard it is to give fair representation to perspectives we personally disagree with. This wasn’t just about the issues at hand, it was a mirror for our own assumptions, and a test of our integrity in the process.

We found that when working as organizational and strategic researchers on issues like child support, the emotions run deep, both within the Child Support Program itself and within us as humans doing the work. Perspectives on poverty, personal autonomy, individual agency, and the role of government collided in ways that brought many tensions to the surface, and we often felt those tensions as sharply as the people we were listening to.

At one point, facing a major impasse, we turned to modeling the most common positions emerging from our sessions. Writing one side came naturally — it reflected our own views. But the opposing voice? We struggled. Early drafts framed it as misguided, even harmful. That moment revealed just how easily bias can seep in, even with the best intentions.

And yet, that struggle was the work.

And yet, that struggle was the work. Wrestling with perspectives we disagreed with forced us to slow down, to listen more carefully, and to understand not just what people believed, but why. It demanded more than empathy — it demanded rigor. We’ve come to believe that this kind of effort should be part of the process itself. Having working groups model both their own and opposing voices, then reflect on that experience, could be transformative. For us, it deepened our respect for every position at the table and gave us a better foundation for moving forward together.

Lessons Learned
#1 Even when every effort is made to listen and honor each voice, some conflicts are rooted so deeply in belief systems, institutional structures, or moral divides that empathy alone cannot bridge them.
#2 Creating neutral models of each perspective helped shift the group from argument to reflection. It gave participants a way to see their own positions more clearly and to recognize the logic in others’ views.
#3 Writing from perspectives that differed from our own revealed our blind spots. The exercise forced us to confront how easily personal beliefs can shape research outputs, even unconsciously.
#4 The discomfort of disagreement and resistance is not a barrier to progress but a source of information about what truly matters to people. Learning to stay with that discomfort, rather than smoothing it over, can produce deeper understanding and more resilient solutions.

Two Truths: Power & Privilege.

Two things are true but rarely discussed in UX: our roles carry both power and privilege. That power is not always visible, but it is embedded in our roles and the decisions we make every day. Designing for others means making choices that can either support or constrain their lives. That responsibility requires care, humility, and an awareness of our influence because everything we create has the potential to shape someone’s life for better or worse.

“All powers have two sides, the power to create and the power to destroy. We must recognize them both, but invest our gifts on the side of creation.” — Robin Wall Kimmerer, Braiding Sweetgrass

Robin Wall Kimmerer is a botanist and member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation whose writing explores reciprocity between humans and the natural world. Her words travel well beyond their original context, and that, too, is worth noticing.

On a project with an automotive company, we conducted qualitative research to understand drivers’ behaviors, needs, and perceptions of electric vehicles. We spoke with EV, hybrid, and gas-powered drivers and uncovered a wide range of deeply held, often conflicting attitudes: some saw driving an EV as something they could personally do to contribute to a better environmental future, while others depended on gas-powered vehicles to do their jobs and support their families.

To capture these tensions, we plotted perspectives on an “In/Tension” scale. Three distinct voices emerged:

It was tempting to connect most with the first voice because it aligned with our own values and lived experiences. But designing only for those who think like us risks reinforcing privilege and overlooking important voices. In/Tension modeling reminds us to ask whether we are designing for people who live like us or for the full range of experiences. It also helps track and map how much each voice can tolerate a given solution, which not only supports more inclusive and sustainable design decisions but also reduces the risk of people abandoning a product or reverting to unhelpful behaviors when a solution pushes beyond what they can accept.

The car example, and the earlier example around child support, show why it is often not the behavior itself that should be judged or dismissed. Our job is to dig deeper to understand why people act the way they do. Why is someone behind on child support payments? Why is someone opposed to EVs? Jumping straight into solutions without that understanding can lead to harm.

A person’s behavior is often shaped by three things: what they are able to do, the circumstances that give them or limit their chances to do it, and the personal drive they feel to act. These elements of capability, opportunity, and motivation work together to influence behaviors. Assuming any of them can cause us to miss the real issue or design a solution that makes things worse. Yet when we understand them, we can remove barriers and, in some cases, help shift an unhelpful behavior into a constructive one.

Following each voice in the EV research revealed these deeper factors. For many EV drivers, the switch aligned with personal values and came with few sacrifices. They drove infrequently, had access to free chargers, and found the change easy. For some gas-powered drivers, however, driving was their livelihood. Charging times meant lost income, and towing for work drained battery life. For them, an EV would threaten their ability to provide for their families.

Understanding these motivations brought empathy into the process. It showed that even when lived experiences differ, the values behind them — responsibility, care for others, doing what is right — can be deeply aligned. It also challenged us to ask a harder question: Are we truly bettering society if our solutions only work for those who already share our worldview? If our work deepens divides rather than bridging them, we may be reinforcing the very systems we hope to improve.

Lessons Learned
#1 Solutions that reflect only our own values and lived experiences risk reinforcing privilege and deepening divides.
#2 Whether someone is behind on child support payments or rejects EVs, the behavior alone is not enough to understand the problem. Deep research into people’s circumstances and constraints offers a clearer view of the “why,” fostering empathy and reducing the risk of harmful assumptions.
#3 Capability, opportunity, and motivation drive behavior. These three factors work together to influence choices. Assuming them can lead to harmful or ineffective solutions, while understanding them can help remove barriers and encourage constructive change.
#4 Mapping how much different perspectives can tolerate a solution allows for more inclusive and sustainable design.
#5 Design should connect people across differences rather than reinforcing existing inequalities. The goal is to bridge, not widen, divides.

When It’s Easier to Choose, and Better Not To

While we as UX professionals play a critical role in confronting power, privilege, and opposing viewpoints in our work, it’s equally important to recognize that we operate within a broader ecosystem — one shaped by human relationships, business objectives, technologies, and cultural norms. For us to effectively practice In/Tension Modeling and ask “What gives us the right?” before “How might we?” we need a culture that supports and protects our ability to create that space.

A recent project offers a compelling example, while translating research insights into new product features for a customer onboarding experience on an e-procurement platform. During synthesis, it was discovered that customers had diverging preferences for how they wanted to add users to their accounts. Some customers knew exactly who they wanted to add and preferred assigning roles and permissions to specific individuals (a user-first approach). Others had a clear idea of the roles and permissions needed but not who would fill them (a role-first approach).

This insight revealed an opportunity to innovate — to meet the needs of those who wanted to assign roles to specific users immediately, and those who needed the flexibility to define roles that could be assigned later. In other words, it was a chance to design for the middle space where tensions and nuance lived.

However, when the author presented these findings to the team, they were asked to “pick a side and recommend it.” Rather than exploring a solution that embraced the tension and expanded the range of tolerance, internal biases and power dynamics took over. The process of translating research into product features shifted — from solving real customer problems across the In/Tension spectrum to prioritizing features that satisfied the preferences of the most powerful stakeholders.

This example shows how cultural forces within teams such as a bias toward quick decisions, deference to power, or discomfort with ambiguity, can collapse the very tension that leads to better, more inclusive outcomes. Practicing In/Tension Modeling isn’t just about having the right methods; it’s about fostering a culture that makes space for complexity, dialogue, and dissent. That kind of culture won’t always be in place, but naming what’s missing is a step toward building it. Even when we can’t fully hold the tension, choosing to surface it is still meaningful. A hope would be that every conversation that resists oversimplification helps shift the culture, bit by bit, toward one that can hold more.

A Practice, Not a Position

So, what gives us the right?

Erika Hall’s question doesn’t have a clean answer, and we’ve stopped expecting one. What we’ve found instead is that the question itself is the practice. Every time we return to it, before a solution, after a finding, in the middle of a disagreement, it keeps us accountable to the people whose lives our work touches. The right, when it exists at all, isn’t ours to keep. We hold it on their behalf, and the work is to be worthy of that.

The work is rarely as simple as deciding who is right and who is wrong. Holding tension does not mean finding the perfect middle ground or choosing which side wins. It means staying curious long enough to understand what different perspectives reveal, particularly when they challenge our own assumptions.

Across every project in this article, child support families navigating an impossible system, drivers weighing livelihood against climate, customers whose needs got flattened into a stakeholder preference, what we found was the same: the most important insights lived exactly where the tension was hardest to hold. Not on either side of it. In it.

We don’t think that changes. We think that’s the work. And we think the practitioners who are willing to stay there, rather than reach for the cleaner answer, are the ones who will build something worth building.

What gives you the right? That question belongs to you now.

title: I Tried Gen Z’s Favorite New Way To Travel—And I Get The Hype
text:
I Tried Gen Z’s Favorite New Way To Travel—And I Get The Hype

I’m one of those people who wants to see the entire world. No flight is too long, no climate is off limits, and yes, I’m still manifesting a trip to Antarctica one day. There are really only two things standing between me and the ever-growing list of destinations in my Notes app: limited PTO and an unfortunately not-unlimited travel budget.

So when I heard about the way Gen Z is squeezing more travel into both, I was intrigued.

Airbnb calls it “lore-tripping”: skipping the obvious vacation destinations in favor of smaller, under-the-radar towns with interesting histories, local legend, and the kind of attractions you probably won’t find replicated in 15 other cities. And apparently, Gen Z is onto something. Airbnb surveyed a group of Gen Z travelers and found that 90% of them are interested in visiting small towns and under-the-radar destinations this fall, drawn by cheaper trips, local culture, and the thrill of finding somewhere that feels still undiscovered.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Best Places To Lore-Trip This Fall:

– Hot Springs, Arizona
– Helen, Georgia
– Point Pleasant, West Virginia
– Twentynine Palms, California
– Rapid City, South Dakota
– Williams, Arizona
– Wildwood, New Jersey
– Gibsonton, Florida
– Leavenworth, Washington
– Bemidji, Minnesota

DashDividers_1_500x100

Instead of automatically booking Paris, Miami, or another destination everyone on your Instagram feed has already visited, the idea is essentially to be the first in your group chat to discover somewhere new.

To chart my own new travel path, Airbnb invited me to spend a weekend lore-tripping in Twentynine Palms, California, a desert town just outside Joshua Tree National Park that is having a moment of its own. According to Airbnb, searches for Twentynine Palms among Gen Z travelers are up more than 50% this fall.

I went into the weekend thinking I was testing a here-today-gone-tomorrow travel trend, but I came back home wondering why I don’t take trips like this more often.

Getting Off The Grid — Literally

The beginning of the drive was familiar. Having made the trip from Los Angeles to Palm Springs for Coachella more times than I’d like to count, I recognized the seemingly endless rows of wind turbines almost immediately. But instead of stopping there, we kept going farther into the California desert, past mountains and those wonderfully strange sculptural Joshua trees until my husband and I reached our home for the weekend in Twentynine Palms.

We arrived at Casa Del Desierto⁠ just after sunset, which, admittedly, made my first introduction to lore-tripping slightly eerie. The house sits in the desert with few neighbors and very little artificial light around it. After living in cities for most of my adult life, I’m accustomed to streetlights, headlights, apartment windows, and the general glow of other human beings being nearby. Out here? Darkness. Desert. Silence.

By the next morning, the unfamiliar lull had become my favorite part.

I woke up before dawn and went outside to sit by the fire pit as the sun came up. The sky slowly turned this almost unbelievable orange-creamsicle shade that looked more like a painting than something happening directly in front of me. I meditated for a while and, for once, managed not to think about the frankly offensive number of unread emails waiting in my inbox. Of course I took pictures. I am still me. But eventually I put my phone down and just sat there.

That became an unexpected theme of the weekend. Lore-tripping made me want to disconnect in the best possible way and to just recharge with nature as the plug.

Now don’t get me wrong, the house definitely helped.

One of the advantages of choosing somewhere less obvious is that your accommodations can become part of the reason you take the trip rather than simply the place where you sleep between activities. Casa Del Desierto was spacious and peaceful, with the kind of indoor-outdoor setup that makes you actually want to stay put. There was a huge bathtub, his-and-hers showers, and the aforementioned fire pit, which quickly became our default spot whenever we had nowhere else to be.

And, because this is Refinery29, I should also mention: There were approximately a million places to take a good outfit photo.

My husband may have summed up the appeal better than I could. He described the desert’s energy as “infectious,” with an eccentric, earthy feeling unlike anywhere else. He loved how quiet it was, and told me he could see himself returning to Joshua Tree anytime he needed to clear his mind.

The stillness even followed him into his workouts. He went running outside, and without the usual soundtrack of traffic, sirens, and people rushing past him, exercise felt surprisingly meditative. My husband described running through the desert as making him feel closer to God: “It’s just me and nature,” he explained when he came back home.

I understood exactly what he meant.

The best part of the trip was finding places I wasn’t looking for. There’s a particular thrill to traveling somewhere famous. You finally see the monument, eat the thing, stand in the spot you’ve seen hundreds of times online. But there’s another kind of pleasure in arriving somewhere with almost no preconceived ideas about what you’re supposed to do.

That’s where lore-tripping really clicked for me.

A short drive from our Airbnb was Más o Menos, which may genuinely be one of the coolest coffee shops I’ve ever visited. I ordered a strawberry-banana matcha while a DJ played Lauryn Hill classics mixed with a ton of other feel-good sounds. And the coffee shop transforms into a 21-and-over hangout at night.

Then there was Kitchen in the Desert. This is one of those places that people should be driving from miles and miles away just to sit at chef Everton Gordon’s table. I have a habit when I travel: Once I find food I love, I will shamelessly go back rather than gambling on somewhere new. So yes, during a weekend-long trip, we ate there twice. The menu was fresh, unexpected, and exactly the kind of discovery that makes you immediately start recommending a place to friends.

None of it felt like we were working through a checklist of Things You Must Do In Twentynine Palms. We were just … there. Exploring. And maybe that’s the real luxury of going somewhere that isn’t overloaded with must-see landmarks.

So would I lore-trip again? Absolutely. I’m not suddenly giving up on Paris (or Antarctica, I’m still coming for you). But this trip changed the way I think about what actually qualifies as a vacation.

There’s a tendency to save our PTO and travel budgets for the big trips: the expensive flights, famous cities, packed itineraries, and destinations that require months of planning. Lore-tripping makes a convincing argument for the spaces in between. A weekend somewhere unexpected can still give you the feeling I’m usually chasing halfway around the world: discovery.

And apparently, I’m not alone. Airbnb says 60% of surveyed travelers are planning a weekend getaway this fall, and its data shows that more weekend trips happened during fall than any other season in 2025.
For travelers trying to see more of the world without unlimited money or vacation days, perhaps the answer isn’t always figuring out how to go farther. That random town you always drive past might be the getaway you never knew you needed.

title: Blakely Thornton on Pop Culture, Gay Beauty Standards, and What Makes An It Girl
text:
Blakely Thornton on Pop Culture, Gay Beauty Standards, and What Makes An It Girl

Blakely Thornton is an original. A self-described Pop Culture Anthropologist and Out 100 Honoree, Blakely has built a digital career that uniquely spans comedy, entertainment, and style. On social media, fans flock to him for his honest, no-holds-barred commentary on their favorite topics. Others tune into Yestergays to hear him and his podcast co-host critique fashion and celebrity culture with his signature wit. Celebrities are smitten with him, often tickled by their engagements at red carpet events like the Met Gala and ultra-exclusive gyms. This very public, creative life wasn’t what Blakely imagined for himself as an athletic kid growing up in Dallas, Texas. Blakely was a closeted football player at UPenn, majoring in finance and hoping to follow in his parents’ footsteps into a respectable, stable career. Headed towards a traditionally corporate career, Blakely worked at Ralph Lauren and pursued the corporate finance life until he didn’t.

Eventually, Blakely decided that he wouldn’t spend another twenty years as anything other than his full self, and it has paid off. Instead of trying to find ways to inject creativity into a 9-5, Blakely leverages his taste and honesty into a living. During our conversation, we cover everything pop culture, from GLP1s to what makes an It Girl to how much attention Zendaya is actually generating for films and fashion houses. We cover the other side of being very popular online, like the mean comments on Reddit, being seen only as a product, and being expected to carry the emotional weight of a fanbase. Blakely is open about the mental and emotional safeguards he needs to manage the opinions of hundreds of thousands of fans, and why he turns to working out to maintain his peace of mind. We also chat about misogynistic beauty standards, how he makes friends with so many celebrities, and why Heated Rivalry was so impactful.

title: Trichologist Ashley Zsaton: Hair Restoration, Growth Supplements & Protective Styles
text:
Trichologist Ashley Zsaton: Hair Restoration, Growth Supplements & Protective Styles

Ashley Zsaton, DNP, ACNP-AG, learned about hair politics early. Growing up biracial in Milwaukee, she wasn’t always accepted for wearing her natural curls. Her search to understand what people meant by “good” and “bad” hair led her to become a board-certified nurse practitioner and hair loss specialist. As co-founder of the Hollywood Hair Institute, California’s preeminent hair transplant & aesthetic treatment center, Dr. Zsaton established herself as a leading hair restoration specialist and trichologist. Her medical background also includes supporting patients in critical conditions in the ICU and in ophthalmology, where her research led to the national publication of a school-based vision screening program. But before she began her medical career, she was trying to develop a healthy relationship with her own hair. A move to the Dominican Republic opened her eyes to the incredible beauty and versatility of naturally curly hair.

In the Dominican Republic, Dr. Zsaton was exposed to a country filled with curly hair styled and cared for in all manner of styles. She brought this newfound passion for hair back to the States, and when she decided to pursue a career in medicine, her husband encouraged her to follow her interest in scalp care towards medical aesthetics. Fast forward to now, and Dr. Zsaton is changing lives by helping people access the hair restoration treatments that are best for them. During our conversation, we discussed every hair restoration treatment from PRP to Follicular Unit Extraction to Minoxidil. Dr. Zsaton walked host, Brooke Devard, through what a good surgical candidate profile looks like, and which alternatives may be a better fit for her patients. In fact, Brooke walked through the exact routine Dr. Zsaton prepared for her and detailed how effective each product has been in growing her hair. Dr. Zsaton doesn’t hold back when it comes to sharing which hairstyles may be causing the most damage, traction alopecia, for both men and women, and which products aren’t doing anything helpful at all. She gives a peek into the aesthetic innovations she’s explored in Turkey and Korea that she’d like to offer her patients here in the States. Dr. Zsaton offered an unfiltered, honest look at the limits and possibilities of hair restoration.

title: Your Horoscope This Week: October 4 To 10
text:
Your Horoscope This Week: October 4 To 10

Cosmic beings, this is our first full week of Venus retrograde in Scorpio, so if relationships suddenly feel moodier, more intense, or a little more dramatic than usual, you can probably chalk some of it up to this retrograde. Venus will remain retrograde until mid-November, giving us plenty of time to revisit what we want from love, friendship, money, beauty, and creativity. Being an observer rather than immediately reacting will help, even if that is much easier said than done under October’s emotionally charged skies. As the week begins, the moon moves through Leo and squares off with the Scorpio energy, which can heighten pride, jealousy, or power struggles. Tend to your own garden and stay in your own lane when you can. There is a highly creative side to this energy too, especially if an old passion, project, aesthetic, or hobby suddenly starts calling your name again.

Midweek, the moon enters Virgo and brings some much-needed grounding to the cosmos. After all that emotional heat, practical tasks may feel strangely therapeutic. This is a good time to tie up loose ends, organize what has gotten messy, and focus on the small choices that help you feel more in control of the direction you want October to take. You do not have to understand every emotion immediately; sometimes cleaning up what is directly in front of you creates enough mental space for the deeper answer to arrive on its own.

Then on October 10th, we welcome the Libra New Moon, bringing considerably lighter energy and inviting us to imagine what the next six months could feel like if we chose greater harmony without abandoning our values. This lunation can help us release grudges, soften frustrations we have been carrying since earlier this year, and reconsider how much conflict we actually want to bring into our next chapter. But because this New Moon is ruled by Venus retrograde in Scorpio, peace cannot come from pretending everything is fine. Our real desires are still part of the conversation. The question this weekend becomes beautifully simple and surprisingly revealing: is the life you are creating actually aligned with what you want, or have you gotten so used to adapting that you stopped asking yourself?

Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Aries Sun & Rising:

Aries, this first full week of Venus retrograde in Scorpio may feel emotionally heavier than your usual pace, because it is activating themes of intimacy, merging, trust, shared resources, and deeper healing. You may become more aware of who you let close, what you carry for other people, or where old relationship patterns still have roots that go further back than the present moment. That level of emotional excavation can feel like a lot for a sign that usually prefers movement over sitting in the feeling, but by the end of the week, you may realize that strength does not always mean handling everything alone.

This weekend, the Libra New Moon brings a lighter reset in your partnership sector and asks you to think about who you actually want beside you for the next six months. Romantic, platonic, and creative partnerships can all come into focus. What would it look like to let the right people in for the right reasons, without abandoning your independence in the process? Set intentions around reciprocity, mutual support, and relationships that make your life feel more expansive rather than more complicated.

Taurus Sun & Rising:

Taurus, with your ruler Venus retrograding through Scorpio in your partnership sector, relationships may feel a little more dramatic, revealing, or emotionally charged than usual this week. You may feel tempted to make quick judgments about who stays, who goes, or what a certain interaction means, but try not to burn bridges before the full story has had time to unfold. Venus retrograde can expose dynamics that were already there, especially around trust, vulnerability, attachment, and power, so let the week show you what needs your attention instead of forcing an immediate conclusion.

Then the Libra New Moon arrives this weekend, and because Libra is also ruled by Venus, your ruler is essentially leading the entire week. This lunation activates your wellness, boundaries, and daily-care sector, reminding you that the way you treat yourself becomes part of the blueprint for how others learn to treat you too. Set intentions around mental, emotional, physical, and spiritual well-being, especially if you have been compromising any of those in the name of companionship. The healthier your relationship with yourself becomes, the clearer your relationship standards become too.

Gemini Sun & Rising:

Gemini, Venus retrograde in Scorpio may make this week feel surprisingly personal even though the focus is on your work, wellness, habits, and daily life. You could become more aware of where your routine is draining you, where resentment has built around responsibilities, or where you have been giving more energy than you are receiving back. Old work dynamics, body-image issues, or habits connected to stress may resurface, but the deeper purpose is to help you understand what your day-to-day life is actually doing to your emotional state.

By the weekend, the Libra New Moon shifts the energy into your romance, creativity, pleasure, and inner-child sector, which can feel like a much-needed breath of fresh air. This lunation asks you to make room for joy on purpose, especially if life has become overly functional lately. Set intentions around dating, creative expression, hobbies, confidence, and anything that reminds you that your life is allowed to feel fun while you are still figuring things out.

Cancer Sun & Rising:

Cancer, Venus retrograde in fellow Water sign Scorpio may make this first full week of the retrograde feel deeply emotional, but also strangely familiar. It is moving through your romance, creativity, pleasure, and inner-child realm, so an old crush, creative passion, or desire you thought you had moved past could suddenly feel relevant again. You may also notice where fear of rejection has made you protect your heart so well that you have accidentally protected yourself from joy too. Let nostalgia give you information without automatically turning it into a sign that you need to recreate the past.

By this weekend, the Libra New Moon activates your home, family, and emotional-foundation sector, inviting you to set intentions around the kind of peace you want to live inside of for the next six months. That could mean making your space more beautiful, creating healthier dynamics with family, or becoming more intentional about what you allow into your private world. After a week of exploring what your heart wants, this New Moon asks an equally important question: does your environment make it easier for that version of you to exist?

Leo Sun & Rising:

Leo, this first full week of Venus retrograde in Scorpio may bring feelings to the surface that are much more private than the version of you everyone else normally gets to see. Venus is moving backward through your home, family, roots, and emotional-security zone, potentially resurfacing childhood memories, family dynamics, old living situations, or relationship patterns that began long before your current circumstances. Scorpio squares your Leo nature, so your first instinct may be to push through the discomfort or regain control quickly. Give yourself enough time to understand what the emotion is connected to before deciding what needs to change.

Then the Libra New Moon this weekend opens a fresh six-month chapter in your communication, learning, and local-community realm. Conversations can become softer, more collaborative, and more productive, especially if this week has shown you how much tone and timing matter. You may want to set intentions around writing, speaking, studying, reconnecting with your neighborhood, or simply becoming someone who communicates what they need before resentment gets the chance to build.

Virgo Sun & Rising:

Virgo, Venus retrograde in Scorpio may have you rereading between the lines this week, and sometimes discovering meaning that you missed the first time around. This retrograde activates your communication, thinking, learning, and immediate-environment sector, so old conversations, messages, sibling dynamics, or ideas can return for another look. You may realize that something you dismissed as insignificant actually aﬀected you more deeply than you admitted, or that you’ve been intellectualizing a feeling because analyzing it felt safer than expressing it. Use your discernment, but resist dissecting every interaction until there is nothing human left in it.

The Libra New Moon arrives this weekend in your money, security, and self-worth sector, helping you turn some of those realizations into tangible intentions. Over the next six months, you may want to create greater financial balance, improve how you price your time and talent, or simply feel more comfortable enjoying what you earn instead of constantly planning for the next emergency. Libra reminds you that stability can include beauty, pleasure, and ease too.

Libra Sun & Rising:

Libra, this first full week of Venus retrograde in Scorpio may have you looking at money and self-worth through a much more emotional lens than usual. Because Venus is your ruler, the retrograde can feel especially personal, and in Scorpio it may bring old spending habits, scarcity fears, or questions around what you are willing to tolerate in exchange for security back to the surface. You could also find yourself reassessing what you value, what you are investing in, and whether certain comforts are actually comforting anymore. Let the week show you where your choices are coming from fear versus genuine desire.

Then the Libra New Moon arrives in your sign this weekend, giving you one of the most personal resets of the year. This is a powerful moment to set intentions around identity, appearance, confidence, relationships, and the way you want to move through the next six months. Because the lunation is ruled by Venus retrograde, you may be starting from a more reflective place than usual, but that can actually make your intentions more honest. Think less about reinventing yourself for other people and more about becoming more recognizable to yourself.

Scorpio Sun & Rising:

Scorpio, Venus retrograding through your sign means this week may feel like a mirror you cannot really look away from. Questions around attraction, identity, relationships, appearance, and desire can become much louder, and you may find yourself revisiting old versions of yourself or wondering why certain people still have such a strong emotional hold. The temptation may be to make dramatic decisions quickly, but this retrograde works better when you let the feelings reveal themselves in layers. You do not need to become a completely different person by the end of the week; you just need to be honest about what no longer feels true.

The Libra New Moon this weekend activates your solitude, subconscious, and healing sector, inviting a much quieter kind of reset. You may feel ready to release a grudge, forgive yourself for something, or simply stop giving so much mental space to a story that has already taken enough from you. This is a beautiful moment to set intentions around rest, spiritual practice, therapy, sleep, and the private habits that help you feel more emotionally regulated. Some of your most important new beginnings may happen where no one else can see them yet.

Sagittarius Sun & Rising:

Sagittarius, Venus retrograde in Scorpio may slow you down just enough to notice what you’ve been trying not to feel. This retrograde is moving through your solitude, healing, and subconscious zone, so old emotions, unfinished relationship stories, dreams, or private fears can resurface in ways that are hard to rationalize away. You may crave more alone time than usual, and that is worth honoring. Rather than treating retreat as stagnation, use the week to notice what your inner world has been asking you to acknowledge.

By the weekend, the Libra New Moon shifts the energy toward friendship, community, and your future goals. This can feel like opening the curtains after spending time in a dim room. You may feel ready to reconnect socially, make plans, join a new group, collaborate, or set intentions around the kind of people you want surrounding your next chapter. After a week of emotional processing, this lunation asks you to imagine what your future could look like if your community reflected who you are becoming now.

Capricorn Sun & Rising:

Capricorn, Venus retrograde in Scorpio may have you looking more closely at the friendships, communities, and long-term goals that have been shaping your future. An old friend, collaborator, or social connection could reappear, but the bigger theme is discerning which relationships still have substance and which ones mostly have history. You may also revisit a dream you once cared deeply about and realize that it still matters, just in a different form. Let the week help you refine your circle and your vision instead of forcing every connection to fit where it used to.

Then the Libra New Moon activates your career, reputation, and public-image zone this weekend, offering a fresh six-month chapter around visibility and ambition. This is a strong moment to set intentions around how you want to be known, what kind of opportunities you want to attract, and which professional relationships could help you get there. Libra energy reminds you that competence matters, but so do diplomacy, presentation, and the way people feel when they work with you.

Aquarius Sun & Rising:

Aquarius, Venus retrograde in Scorpio may make you rethink what success actually looks like when no one else is defining it for you. This retrograde moves through your career and public-image realm, so an old professional goal, former collaborator, missed opportunity, or complicated feeling about recognition could return for another look. You may notice where ambition has become tangled up with validation, or where you have been maintaining a path simply because it once made sense. Give yourself permission to question the blueprint before deciding what still deserves your effort.

By the weekend, the Libra New Moon lights up your expansion, travel, education, publishing, and belief zone, which can feel much more spacious. Set intentions around learning something new, seeing more of the world, sharing your ideas with a larger audience, or saying yes to experiences that stretch your perspective. You could revisit travel plans, education, spirituality, publishing, or even a connection tied to another place or chapter of your life. Let yourself explore why something still has emotional weight before deciding whether it belongs in your future.

title: How These Latine Creators Turned Internet Fame Into Lasting Careers
text:
How These Latine Creators Turned Internet Fame Into Lasting Careers

For a generation of creatives, the Internet has become both a canvas and a launchpad. Bedrooms, timelines, and feeds have been turned into places where entire careers can begin. And sometimes, the work starts to stretch beyond the platform that first made it visible and the question becomes, “what happens when you want to build beyond the thing people first knew you for?” For the creatives who came up online, that can mean taking an audience into a new medium, turning influence into ownership, or simply giving themselves permission to become someone new.

We spoke with six Latine creatives working across poetry, music, entertainment, beauty, and brand-building about the leap from being known online to building something that can live beyond it. Their paths look wildly different, but the same thread runs through them: The work that lasts until the end comes from somewhere deeper than the digital binary. It comes from following what’s in your heart, trusting the parts of yourself that feel most true, and carrying who you are and where you come from with you as everything else changes.

Desi Perkins — Beauty Creator & Founder of DEZI and DEZI Skin

It all started as a passion project. I had no idea it could become a career. The moment everything changed was my first collaboration with an eyewear brand. It was the first product I had ever created to sell, and it did $7 million in 12 minutes. We completely shutdown Shopify and exceeded every expectation anyone had. I remember being genuinely shocked because I had no idea I could sell anything, let alone at that scale. Until that day, I don’t think I fully understood how much support I had behind me. That experience made me realize that I could take the community and trust I had built online and create something tangible from it. It also showed me the difference between contributing to something and owning what you’re building. I wanted more than my name attached to a product. I wanted a seat at every table — product development, operations, marketing, finances — and to build something where the long-term value belonged to me and my family. 

An audience can help you have a successful launch, but it cannot guarantee you a sustainable company. I never wanted to create a product just because I knew people would buy it once. I wanted them to finish it, miss it when it was gone, and spend their own money to buy it again. Building DEZI Skin forced me to think beyond hype. Going slowly taught me that trust can get someone through the door, but the product has to earn the repeat purchase. Influence can create attention, but it cannot replace a strong product, healthy margins, good operations, or customer loyalty. People also underestimate how much creators learn by being in direct conversation with consumers every single day. We know what people are asking, the problems they’re trying to solve, what language connects, and when something feels forced. But understanding the consumer doesn’t automatically mean you know how to run a company. I had to learn forecasting, inventory, cash flow margins, retail partnerships, hiring, and operations—all the things no one sees in a launch post. 

I used to think longevity meant staying relevant. Now I think it means building something that doesn’t depend entirely on my relevance. Platforms will change. Algorithms will change. People’s attention will move somewhere else. I’m building brands with real products, real teams, retail relationships, and customers who may discover DEZI without knowing anything about my YouTube career. I’m also building equity. Something my family can benefit from long after a post stops performing. 

That ownership is personal to me in other ways, too. Being Mexican-American doesn’t look or sound one specific way, and there were moments when people made me feel like I wasn’t Latina enough. With DEZI Skin, I didn’t want to translate my identity into something more comfortable or marketable for everyone else. The Spanglish, the ingredients, the product names, and the stories are all connected to how I actually grew up. The goal isn’t to remove myself from the story. It’s to build [the brands] strongly enough that they can grow beyond me.

Katteyes — Creator & Recording Artist

I’ve always loved music. When I was very young, I went to singing academies, and when I was 14, I released a couple of songs and then deleted them because I was embarrassed. By the time I was 18, after already building most of my career as a digital creator, I decided to pursue music because it had always been a passion of mine, but I hadn’t felt ready or prepared before. I didn’t know how to release music or upload it to platforms, and I signed my first music contract without really understanding what I was signing. I come from a working-class neighborhood in Chile. I went to public school, and I had to learn almost everything on my own. I made a lot of mistakes, but because of them, I learned how to manage my career today. When I decided to focus on music, I basically had to start again from zero.

Having followers who watch you for 15 seconds on a social platform is completely different from getting someone to listen to your music for three minutes and then go find you on Spotify, Apple Music, or another platform. More than moving an audience from one place to another, I had to build a new audience. When I started releasing music, I stopped creating digital content for a full year and stopped accepting campaigns. My income dropped a lot because I was betting on this new project and taking that risk. I had to reinvent myself. Social media and music are completely different worlds, but I do think they can complement each other, and everything I learned from the speed of the digital world has helped me understand the artistic world, too. 

As an artist, I’ve realized there can be a lot of anxiety and frustration around always asking, “What’s next?” Instead of chasing viral moments or trying to copy-and-paste the same successful song, I believe in following your essence and making what you actually love, what fills your heart. That’s what brings results because you’re making something unique and authentic. I want everything I do to feel 100% mine, whether I’m involved in the choreography, the technical production, the visuals, or every detail of a show. And no matter how international my music or image becomes, I always want people to know I’m Chilean. I carry Chile with me everywhere I go. More than visibility, I think what builds something lasting is not being afraid of rejection, of being laughed at, or of looking ridiculous. You have to show yourself authentically. That’s how you create a fandom, a family that can follow you for years because they connect with who you really are.

Kathleen Lights — Beauty Creator & Founder of Lights Lacquer

I think [what has allowed my career to last] has been my ability to stay relatable and authentic. I’ve been pretty open about my struggles with anxiety and have shared a lot of my life with my audience, the good and the not-so-great—and I think people resonate with that. Makeup was what brought us together, but those conversations allowed the connection to become more personal. I’m also very honest in my reviews, and my audience appreciates that. People are spending their money based on something I recommend, and I take that seriously. When I started my channel, I was mainly looking for community. I was excited to gain subscribers, but I never imagined it could turn into the business it has become. Working with brands helped me realize how much I enjoyed product development and showed me I could do more than review products; I could help create them. But having an audience and building a business are very different things. I’m incredibly grateful that my community gave me a place to start, but I don’t see their support as something I’m automatically entitled to. I wanted to create products people would genuinely enjoy, not something they would purchase only because they wanted to support me.

Ownership and creative control are everything when you’re attaching your name to a brand. Having your name attached to a brand and having the ability to shape its direction aren’t necessarily the same thing. That’s why I launched Lights Lacquer on my own. I wanted to be closely involved in the products, the stories behind the collections, and the experience we’re giving our customers. I’ve loved being able to build a brand with my audience in mind, but ultimately, I want someone who has never watched a KathleenLights video to discover Lights Lacquer and love it. My audience helped give the brand its beginning, but the products need to give people a reason to come back. [My Cuban-American identity] is woven into so much of it because it’s how I grew up and I hope another Latina can see that there’s room to build something without separating yourself from where you come from. After more than a decade online, my definition of success has become more personal. I don’t want to measure everything by whether I’m getting more attention than I was yesterday. If I’m making work I’m proud of, maintaining that connection with my community, and feeling okay in my actual life, that means a lot to me. 

Laith Ashley — Creator, Model, & Actor

It’s quite interesting, especially thinking retrospectively about how far social media has come in the last 10 to 15 years. Instagram was still in its infancy. It had not developed into the content creator market that we see today. For the most part, I was posting myself, my friends, and my family. When a photo of mine suddenly went viral overnight, it felt like I was thrust into the public eye and was unprepared for what that came with. I was fortunate enough to receive overwhelming support after the initial backlash. As opportunities began coming my way, I told myself I had to take them despite my fear, and I am glad I did. I have tried my best [to expand beyond what people first discovered me for], but it’s hard to break free from the boxes you are put in based on how you’re perceived, especially if you’re POC. There are moments I have struggled to be seen beyond my body, especially as I age. I have, however, realized that all I am and can be are also tools I can use to further my career. I cannot control every aspect of how I am perceived, and that isn’t my job. People are going to believe what they want to believe. I spent a long time trying to convince people of one thing or another. That was exhausting, to say the least.

I’m not ashamed of my transness. When I’ve spoken about wanting to be recognized beyond it, it was because every single thing I did was punctuated by it, even if it had nothing to do with gender identity. I knew that at the time visibility was important, and it still is. The issue I had was that I wasn’t allowed to perform beyond it. At this point in my life and career, I feel like I am rediscovering myself, my passions, and what brings me joy, and that has also been a lot of work. Messy work! My relationship with social media has changed tremendously, too. There are moments when I feel like I have aged out of social media or have lost interest altogether—maybe I’m just tired. [My advice is to] have fun, be yourself, and stay informed. I spent so much time chasing this idea of success that I missed out on living in the moment and enjoying those small victories and time spent with really amazing people.

Maleni Cruz — Creator, Comedic Actor, & Recording Artist

I don’t think I ever realized my audience could become something bigger. Even now, I don’t know if I fully realize it. The moment that really hit me was when people started naming their kids after me. I was like, “okay, if y’all are naming you’re kids after me, I can’t fail you!” When people tell me they’ve been watching me for so long that they feel connected to me, that connection is never going to go away. When people grow with you and experience life with you, that’s how you know they’re going to support you time and time again. I think what has helped me build that is how authentic I am. People relate to me so much, they think they’re talking to their cousin, their sister, their homegirl. When they see me, they feel like they’ve known me for years. Before content became my full-time career, I was still working in dance, and I got to a point where I couldn’t give 100% to that job and 100% to myself. I had to bet on myself. I had to ask, “Are you picking yourself or are you going to neglect you?” It was time to really pour into myself.

I’m still building what I want my career to look like. I want to do more acting, more comedy, even action comedy. I want to be recognized for my talent because I really see myself as a performer and an entertainer. But I’m also a firm believer that whatever door is in front of you, take it. You really don’t know where those doors are going to lead you. That’s how I’ve been my whole life, even before social media. Being from New York and being Dominican are things that are always going to walk with me. That’s just who I am. My advice to anyone starting out is to do whatever makes you happy and post whatever makes you happy. Don’t think too much about what someone else is doing, how many views something has, or how many comments it gets. If you follow what your heart wants to do, regardless of what everyone else thinks you should or shouldn’t be doing, just do it.

Orion Carloto — Creator & Author

It’s funny how often I reflect on [those early years online], and how it always comes down to the belief that the Internet saved my life in some strange way. I found little corners in the world where I could create a shrine of everything I already knew and loved, which inevitably led me down rabbit holes of shinier obsessions. You could shape a world and let a new world shape you. There was fear in letting people into the real me, so it was natural that I went out seeking kindred oddballs. Growing up in a predominantly white town, it was also the Internet that led me to love my identity in more ways than one. It was in this strange absence of closeness (to others) that I went looking for communities more like me.

I just wanted an ear, and I’m grateful that people are kind enough to still keep listening. There’s a sense of entanglement I share with my audience that feels less like “an audience” and more like, “Oh, we just grew up together.” We’re all interested in the same things. For me, longevity has come down to being honest with myself. If your heart is in something, other people will feel that too. Feeling is extremely important to me. Documenting feeling. Documenting change. I’ll take the photo, I’ll write a poem, I’ll journal about the cicadas, I’ll pocket a spoon from an Amarillo Motel. I love road movies about nothing. My favorite genre of literature is reading about how someone felt about something. Anything. I’m interested. But I think we all are. The language is in the everyday, and the everyday outlives us all. Doing this has taught me that.
